wines.name: Granbazán Etiqueta Ámbar Albariño 2024
wines.sub: Rías Baixas DO · Val do Salnés, Galicia, Spain
wines.flag: The amber label is the house classic. Etiqueta Ámbar made Granbazán's name in the 1990s and was poured by the glass at El Bulli for years. The back label confirms 8 months on fine lees.
factors: Cool, wet maritime. Val do Salnés is the coldest, rainiest and most Atlantic of the Rías Baixas subzones. High rainfall and humidity mean rot risk; acidity stays high.
Vines in the region are traditionally trained on high pergolas (parras), which lift the grapes off the damp ground for airflow and reduce rot.
Free-draining granite and sand, which helps in such a wet climate and gives a stony, saline character.
Albariño: thick skins (resists rot), high acid, aromatic but not overpowering: peach, citrus, flowers, a salty finish.
Over 40 years old: half estate-grown, half from local families who have farmed Albariño for generations.

Destemmed, a few hours of cold skin contact, free-run juice only. Fermented in temperature-controlled steel, then about 8 months on the lees with more stirring (bâtonnage) than Granbazán's other wines. More texture and weight than a basic Albariño.
Winemaker Diego Ríos spent time in the Mosel working with Riesling, which shows in the wine's acid structure.
wines.concl: Very good. High, Riesling-like acidity balanced by ripe stone fruit and lees texture; intense and long for its price.
exam: Rías Baixas subzones: Val do Salnés (coolest, wettest), O Rosal and Condado do Tea (warmer, inland along the Miño).
Pergola training: airflow and rot control in a humid climate.
Lees ageing with bâtonnage adds body and creaminess without oak.
pair: Oysters, clams, pulpo a la gallega
wines.say: The Albariño El Bulli poured by the glass: lime, white peach and sea salt, with extra body from eight months on its lees.

wines.name: Domaine Thibert Les Longeays 2019
facts: 23 months, partly in new French oak
wines.flag: Read the back label. This is the 2019, aged 23 months partly in new French oak, with native yeast and no filtration. Generic producer sheets describe a mostly steel-aged wine; this importer's bottling is richer. Expect toast, vanilla and seven years of development. The bottle sells for $59, so $21 a glass is a good deal.
factors: Moderate continental. The Mâconnais is the warmest, sunniest part of Burgundy, so its Chardonnay is riper and rounder than Côte d'Or or Chablis.
2019 was hot and dry in Burgundy, with low yields. The whites are concentrated and ripe, but acidity held up better than expected.
Clay-limestone, well drained, on the right bank of the Valouse stream. Limestone keeps a mineral, saline edge.
Planted in 1975. Fifty-year-old vines give low yields and concentrated fruit.

Hand-picked, native-yeast fermentation, then 23 months of ageing, partly in new French oak, and bottled unfiltered. New oak adds vanilla, toast and some tannic grip; the long ageing adds texture and early development.
Family estate founded in 1967 in Fuissé, nearly 30 ha, now run by Christophe and Sandrine Thibert. This bottling is the importer Pierreclos's selection.
wines.concl: Very good, possibly outstanding. Ripe 2019 fruit balanced by fresh acidity; new oak and seven years of age add layers of secondary and tertiary complexity; long, saline finish.
wines.ready: Drink now: in its drinking window. Can hold a few more years, not designed for long ageing.
exam: Mâconnais hierarchy: Mâcon → Mâcon-Villages → village AOCs (Pouilly-Fuissé, Pouilly-Vinzelles, Saint-Véran, Viré-Clessé).
The label's "cru" means a named vineyard. Only Pouilly-Fuissé has official Premier Crus in the Mâconnais (since the 2020 vintage).
Spot the development: primary fruit, secondary oak and MLF, tertiary honey and nuts. Calling all three is how you earn "Developing" on the SAT.
pair: Roast chicken, veal in cream sauce
wines.say: A seven-year-old Mâconnais Chardonnay from 1975 vines, aged nearly two years in oak: rich pear, toast and hazelnut. Meursault-style richness at a fraction of the price.

wines.name: Domaine du Gros 'Noré Bandol Rosé 2025
wines.flag: Imported by Kermit Lynch, one of the great champions of Provence and Bandol. Alain Pascal is a former boxer who sold his grapes to other estates before bottling his own in 1997.
factors: Warm Mediterranean, but the amphitheatre of slopes faces the sea, and the Mistral and sea breezes cool the vines. Mourvèdre, a very late ripener, needs this heat to ripen.
Clay and limestone terraces around La Cadière d'Azur. Poor, well-drained soils hold yields low (about 30 hl/ha).
Mourvèdre gives structure, savoury herbs and age-worthiness. Cinsault adds freshness and red fruit; Grenache adds body and strawberry.
Recent vintages: Grenache and Cinsault get a short maceration, Mourvèdre is direct-pressed, then blended. Fermented in concrete or steel, no wood, bottled in spring.
wines.concl: Very good. Structured, savoury and long for a rosé; Mourvèdre gives grip and weight that most Provence pinks lack.
wines.ready: Drink now, but has potential for ageing (a few years).
exam: Bandol: red must be at least 50% Mourvèdre with 18 months in oak; rosé and white also made.
Mourvèdre: late-ripening, needs heat; gives tannin, dark fruit and gamey or herbal savouriness in reds.
Most Provence rosé is pale and light; Bandol is the structured, age-worthy exception.
wines.say: Provence rosé with backbone: Mourvèdre-led Bandol, savoury and salty, with blood orange and herbs. It can even age.

wines.name: Les Deux Flèches Moulin-à-Vent Vierre Manin 2024
wines.flag: Vierre Manin is a named vineyard (lieu-dit) in Moulin-à-Vent. The winemaking notes below come from the producers' main Moulin-à-Vent: mostly destemmed, little carbonic maceration, neutral barrels. This single-site bottling may differ in the details. The micro-estate is run by Nicolas and Jérémy, teachers at the Davayé wine school.
factors: Moderate continental, slightly warmer than the Côte d'Or. Gamay ripens fully here in normal years.

2024 was late and wet: a cold, rainy spring disrupted flowering, mildew and black rot cut yields, and a cool September delayed the harvest. Reds are fresh, fruity and lighter. Hence only 12.5% alcohol.
Thin topsoil over hard pink granite, rich in manganese and iron. The manganese is said to limit yields and give smaller, thicker-skinned berries: more colour and tannin than other crus.
Gamay: thin-skinned, high acid, low-to-medium tannin, red fruit and floral notes.

Producers' usual approach: mostly destemmed, native yeasts, concrete fermentation, little to no carbonic maceration, then ageing in mostly neutral French oak. Fewer banana/bubblegum notes, more structure.
wines.concl: Good to very good. Bright, tangy fruit and fine tannin in balance; floral and herbal notes add interest. Lighter than a typical Moulin-à-Vent, as the vintage would predict.
wines.ready: Drink now. Could hold 3–5 years, but 2024 favours freshness over long ageing.
exam: The 10 Beaujolais crus; Moulin-à-Vent is the most structured and age-worthy, and the crus may be sold as Bourgogne.
Carbonic and semi-carbonic maceration give kirsch, banana and bubblegum notes; destemmed fermentation gives more structure.
2024 links three of our wines: Pernot, Guérin and this Moulin-à-Vent all come from the same wet, mildew-hit vintage, all lighter and fresher.
wines.say: The most serious Beaujolais cru, made like Burgundy: cherry and rose, with real grip from pink granite.

lineup.sub: A Galician Albariño, a seven-year-old oaked Mâconnais Chardonnay, a Mourvèdre-led Bandol rosé and a single-site Moulin-à-Vent from the wet 2024 vintage.
rows: Rosé drinkers who want a food wine

blocks.title: Tasting order for a flight
items: Albariño → Bandol Rosé → Les Longeays → Moulin-à-Vent.
The rosé goes before the Thibert: after 23 months in oak and seven years in bottle, the Chardonnay would overpower it.

blocks.title: Across the library
items: Three rosés now: Cuomo (short maceration, Aglianico), Boudignon (direct press, Cabernet Franc), Gros 'Noré (Mourvèdre, mixed method). Compare colour and body.
Thibert 2019 vs Pernot 2024: new oak and bottle age vs used barrels and youth. Practise calling development.
Moulin-à-Vent vs Guérin Pinot vs Verduno Nebbiolo: the tannin ladder.
